extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television critics, and fans of British TV comedy-drama
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative dimensions used to judge an anthology British television comedy-drama (Inside No. 9), as reflected in critical reception and reporting. Focuses on writing, acting, tone, production choices, audience reception, and awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast and acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise directed at the cast and acting (frequently commended across episodes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics repeatedly single out performances (e.g., praise for cast and acting in 'Sardines', Alison Steadman's performance in 'Séance Time'); strong acting is treated as a central measure of episode quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripting / writing quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of the scripts — plotting, characterisation, and dialogue — is a primary evaluative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'intriguing and lovingly-crafted' scripts, high praise for 'The 12 Days of Christine' as a 'masterpiece' with an emotional script and poignancy; scripts of some episodes were singled out as weaker, affecting overall reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of the twist ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a twist ending works for the episode — some twists receive mixed responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics had a 'mixed response to the twist ending' in episodes such as 'Sardines' — a good twist can elevate reception, a poor or forced twist can draw criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour style and inventiveness (including physical comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: How funny and inventive the comedic elements are, including use of physical comedy and comic timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'A Quiet Night In' relied on physical comedy and was 'well received as funny, and inventive'; humour is also noted as extremely personal, so reception can vary by critic/audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot strength and narrative coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the plot is constructed and whether it coheres and satisfies dramatic/comedic aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Tom & Gerri' was commended for its plot despite being less comedic; 'The Understudy' praised for plot divergence from Macbeth while remaining enjoyable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of sensitive subjects (e.g., mental illness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the depiction of sensitive themes (mental illness, horror, celebrity culture) is handled appropriately and thoughtfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics 'disagreed about the portrayal of mental illness' in 'Tom & Gerri', indicating that handling of delicate topics affects critical judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone balance (comedy vs horror / darkness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The programme's ability to balance comedic and horrific/somber elements and shift tone appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes varied from 'less horrific' to 'the most horrific episode' ('The Harrowing' considered genuinely scary); critics note that the anthology's shifts in tone are central to its identity and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional impact and poignancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional resonance of scripts and the poignancy of endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'The 12 Days of Christine' was praised for emotional script and poignancy; strong emotional payoff is cited as a hallmark of the best episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness: telling fully formed stories in limited runtime
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to deliver 'perfectly formed narratives' with proper backstories and unwinding scenarios within roughly 30 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rachel Cooke praised the writers' ability to 'squeeze perfectly formed narratives... into just 30 minutes' — economy of storytelling is a positive criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty and imaginative conception of episodes and premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'the rich and perverse imaginations' of the creators and 'consistently compelling' and 'original' — originality in premise and approach is repeatedly lauded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility and range
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers' and series' ability to display a wide range of styles, genres and formats across episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics praised the writers' 'versatility and ability with the atypical setting and language' and the fact 'each episode is different from the last'; versatility is considered a strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production and filming style / formal innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of unusual filming techniques or production innovations and how successfully they serve the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'unusual filming style' of some episodes was commended; the show used techniques like split-screen, silent episodes, virtual studio production and a live Halloween episode, which critics treated as notable creative risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode endings (resolution and audience satisfaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: How well episodes resolve and whether endings satisfy or polarise viewers/critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There was a 'mixed response to the episode's ending' for several episodes; the quality of an ending (twist, poignancy, shock) strongly shapes critical reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scare factor for horror-leaning episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of horror elements in generating genuine fear or dread where intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'The Harrowing' described as 'genuinely scary' by critics — for episodes leaning into horror, authentic fright is a key success metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility despite literary or intertextual bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether episodes borrowing from plays/literature remain accessible to viewers unfamiliar with those sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though 'The Understudy' was based on Macbeth, 'a knowledge of the play was not necessary for enjoyment' — accessibility is praised when adaptations diverge cleverly yet remain enjoyable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-taking and formal experiments (e.g., silent episode, live broadcast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Willingness to experiment with format and take creative risks, and whether those experiments succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics noted and evaluated experiments such as a silent episode, a live Halloween episode and episodes filmed in nonstandard ways; successful experiments earn praise and can be distinguishing features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation and ability to attract talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Show's reputation as measured by its ability to attract well-known actors and guest stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writers' reputation 'helped attract actors' who might not commit otherwise; returning guest stars and high-profile cameo casting are noted as indicators of standing and production quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical consensus and awards recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by critics and awards (nominations/wins) as evidence of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The series' 100% Rotten Tomatoes score, multiple awards (Rose d'Or, BAFTA nominations/wins, etc.) and critics' praise are reported as validating measures of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewing figures and audience reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative audience metrics (overnight/7-day/28-day viewers) and broader audience reach as indicators of popularity and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite critical acclaim, the first series had relatively poor viewing figures; critics and producers note the tension between critical success and mass audience numbers.
